title: Alteplase: Bleeding Risk and Neuro Change
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Alteplase is a fibrinolytic used in selected acute ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism settings. The major nursing danger is serious bleeding, especially intracranial hemorrhage; sudden headache, vomiting, worsening neurologic deficit, hypotension, or new bleeding requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Fibrinolysis dissolves pathologic fibrin but also increases bleeding risk.
In stroke pathways, eligibility and timing depend on strict acute-care criteria and brain imaging.
priorities: Verify that the thrombolysis checklist and required screening have been completed by the acute-care team.
Minimize invasive procedures after treatment when possible.
Perform frequent neurologic, blood-pressure, and bleeding assessments according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend neurologic status, blood pressure, puncture sites, urine/stool, gums, bruising, and any sudden pain or decline.
interventions: Maintain emergency readiness for hemorrhage and airway compromise.
Follow post-thrombolysis restrictions and imaging/lab protocol.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet timing after thrombolysis is protocol-driven.
Do not assume a small external bleed is the only bleeding site when neurologic or hemodynamic status is changing.
teaching: Explain that close neurologic and bleeding monitoring is expected after treatment.
delegationScope: Thrombolytic administration and monitoring require facility competency and state-defined scope; acute changes require immediate RN/provider/stroke-team escalation.
examTrap: Continuing routine invasive procedures after fibrinolysis despite avoidable bleeding risk.
oneLinePearl: After alteplase, every new neuro change is hemorrhage until evaluated.

title: Tenecteplase: Single-Bolus Thrombolytic Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Tenecteplase is a fibrinolytic administered as an IV bolus for approved acute thrombotic indications. Because the dose is weight-based and the drug can cause catastrophic bleeding, patient identity, current weight, indication-specific protocol, recent surgery/bleeding history, blood pressure, and concurrent antithrombotic therapy must be checked before administration.
recognize: The single-bolus format does not make the medication low risk.
Neurologic decline or unexplained hypotension after thrombolysis can represent occult hemorrhage.
priorities: Verify indication-specific eligibility and dose calculation with the required independent check.
Monitor closely for neurologic and systemic bleeding after administration.
Escalate any acute neurologic deterioration or major bleeding immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend neurologic status, blood pressure, puncture sites, hemoglobin when ordered, and evidence of internal bleeding.
interventions: Limit unnecessary invasive procedures and apply prolonged pressure to required puncture sites.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute tenecteplase and alteplase regimens because dosing and administration differ.
Concurrent anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding risk.
teaching: Tell the patient to report severe headache, sudden weakness, chest/abdominal pain, or bleeding immediately.
delegationScope: Thrombolytic administration and monitoring authority varies by facility/state and requires high-alert competency.
examTrap: Treating tenecteplase as interchangeable with alteplase because both are thrombolytics.
oneLinePearl: One bolus can still cause one catastrophic bleed—verify everything before pushing.

title: Nitroprusside: Continuous Pressure and Toxicity Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sodium nitroprusside is a very rapid arterial and venous vasodilator that can cause precipitous hypotension and cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity. It requires continuous blood-pressure monitoring and controlled infusion in a setting capable of immediate response.
recognize: Excessive hypotension can cause cerebral, coronary, or renal ischemia.
Prolonged or high-exposure therapy increases cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity risk, especially with organ dysfunction.
priorities: Use continuous hemodynamic monitoring and an infusion pump.
Protect/dilute the medication exactly according to product and facility requirements.
Escalate unexplained metabolic acidosis, altered mentation, cardiovascular instability, or apparent loss of drug effect.
assessMonitor: Trend continuous BP, heart rate, perfusion, mental status, acid-base data when indicated, and renal/hepatic function.
interventions: Titrate only under a validated critical-care order/protocol and competency.
Reduce or stop infusion promptly for dangerous hypotension according to protocol.
medicationSafety: The concentrate is not for direct injection and requires dilution.
Continuous pressure monitoring is a label-level safety requirement.
teaching: Explain that intensive monitoring is required because the medication acts within minutes.
delegationScope: Nitroprusside titration generally requires critical-care competency and facility/state authorization; the PN's role may be limited to monitoring and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Running nitroprusside without continuous BP monitoring because the patient looked stable at the start.
oneLinePearl: Nitroprusside can drop pressure fast and poison slowly—monitor both.

title: Nicardipine Infusion: Controlled Blood-Pressure Reduction
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV nicardipine is a titratable dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker used when rapid controlled blood-pressure reduction is needed. The goal is controlled reduction without causing hypotension, reflex tachycardia, or loss of organ perfusion.
recognize: Too-rapid BP reduction can worsen cerebral, coronary, or renal perfusion.
Peripheral IV sites can develop irritation/phlebitis during continuous infusion.
priorities: Use frequent or continuous BP monitoring according to acuity.
Assess neurologic status, chest symptoms, urine output, and perfusion while BP changes.
Follow the ordered titration target rather than chasing a normal number.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, heart rate, neurologic status, renal perfusion, edema, and infusion-site condition.
interventions: Use infusion-pump controls and facility titration protocol.
Rotate/inspect peripheral access according to product and facility guidance.
medicationSafety: Avoid uncontrolled rapid lowering in patients whose organ perfusion depends on higher pressure.
Heart failure, hepatic/renal impairment, and ischemic symptoms require close monitoring.
teaching: Explain that treatment targets safe controlled pressure reduction, not instant normalization.
delegationScope: Continuous vasoactive-infusion titration requires facility/state competency; the PN monitors and escalates within authorized scope.
examTrap: Trying to normalize severely elevated BP immediately instead of following the ordered gradual target.
oneLinePearl: Nicardipine is controlled pressure reduction, not a race to normal.

title: Dexmedetomidine: Sedation With Bradycardia Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist sedative that can provide arousable sedation but may cause significant bradycardia and hypotension. Continuous monitoring and careful response assessment are essential, especially in patients with conduction disease, hypovolemia, or other rate-slowing therapy.
recognize: Patients may remain rousable despite adequate sedation.
Bradycardia and hypotension can become clinically important and require prompt intervention.
priorities: Monitor heart rate, BP, oxygenation, sedation level, and perfusion.
Assess whether oversedation, bradycardia, or hypotension is worsening clinical status.
Escalate severe bradycardia, syncope, or hemodynamic instability.
assessMonitor: Continuous ECG/hemodynamic monitoring in critical-care use; trend sedation goal, respiratory status, and withdrawal symptoms after prolonged exposure.
interventions: Use controlled infusion equipment and the ordered sedation protocol.
Address hypovolemia or interacting medications with the critical-care team.
medicationSafety: A 2026 labeling update revised warnings/precautions; current product labeling should be used at administration.
Although respiratory depression is often less than with many sedatives, airway monitoring remains necessary.
complications: Hypertension during loading in some patients
teaching: Explain that the patient may be sleepy but still able to respond and that monitoring continues throughout sedation.
delegationScope: Sedative-infusion titration requires defined critical-care competency; LPN/LVN authority varies by jurisdiction/facility.
examTrap: Assuming a sedated but arousable patient is undertreated and escalating sedation without checking the ordered target.
oneLinePearl: Dexmedetomidine can spare breathing but slow the heart—monitor both.

title: Propofol: Airway, Pressure, and Strict Handling
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Propofol is a rapid IV sedative/anesthetic that can cause apnea, hypotension, bradycardia, and loss of airway reflexes. Administration requires personnel able to continuously monitor and rescue the airway and circulation, plus strict aseptic handling because the lipid emulsion can support microbial growth.
recognize: BP can fall quickly after bolus or infusion changes.
Prolonged high-dose exposure can contribute to propofol infusion syndrome with metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, renal failure, and cardiovascular collapse.
priorities: Ensure airway/resuscitation equipment and continuous monitoring are available.
Assess sedation depth, respiratory status, BP, heart rate, and perfusion.
Escalate unexplained acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, or cardiovascular deterioration during prolonged infusion.
assessMonitor: Continuous oxygenation, ventilation, hemodynamics, sedation target; triglycerides and metabolic markers when clinically indicated during prolonged infusion.
interventions: Use strict aseptic technique and product-specific tubing/container change requirements.
medicationSafety: Propofol is not an analgesic; pain must be treated separately.
Do not assume spontaneous breathing means airway reflexes and ventilation are adequate.
teaching: Explain that close airway and blood-pressure monitoring is required throughout sedation.
delegationScope: Propofol administration is highly restricted by state/facility policy and competency; do not assume routine LPN/LVN authority.
examTrap: Using propofol for pain control because the patient appears comfortable while sedated.
oneLinePearl: Propofol sedates fast, drops pressure fast, and does not treat pain.
sourceBasis: DailyMed propofol injectable emulsion labeling updated 2026-05/06

title: Vasopressin: Vasodilatory Shock Support
bottomLine: Vasopressin is used to raise blood pressure in adults with vasodilatory shock that remains hypotensive despite fluids and catecholamines. It can reduce perfusion to coronary, mesenteric, skin, and digital beds, so BP improvement must be interpreted together with organ perfusion.
recognize: Potential adverse effects include bradycardia, tachyarrhythmia, hyponatremia, decreased cardiac output, and ischemia.
A higher blood pressure does not guarantee better tissue perfusion.
priorities: Monitor BP, rhythm, skin/digital perfusion, abdominal symptoms, urine output, and mental status.
Use controlled infusion and the prescribed shock protocol.
Escalate new ischemic pain, mottling, arrhythmia, or worsening perfusion.
assessMonitor: Trend MAP/BP target, heart rhythm, sodium, lactate/perfusion markers when ordered, urine output, and extremity/mesenteric ischemia clues.
interventions: Maintain reliable vascular access and inspect for complications.
Reassess overall shock response rather than titrating to BP alone.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 labeling specifies dilution and infusion use for vasodilatory shock.
Abrupt hemodynamic changes require immediate review of pump, line, and patient status.
teaching: Explain that the infusion supports blood pressure while the underlying shock cause is treated.
delegationScope: Vasoactive-infusion titration is restricted by competency and state/facility policy; PN monitoring/escalation duties remain essential where involved.
examTrap: Calling vasopressin effective solely because MAP improved while the extremities became cold and mottled.
oneLinePearl: Pressure up is not enough—check whether organs are perfusing.

title: Dobutamine: Inotropy With Rhythm Monitoring
bottomLine: Dobutamine is a short-term inotrope used when depressed myocardial contractility is causing inadequate cardiac output. It may improve perfusion but can increase heart rate, ectopy, myocardial oxygen demand, and ischemia, so rhythm and hemodynamic response must be monitored continuously.
recognize: Expected benefit is improved cardiac output/perfusion rather than simply a higher heart rate.
Tachyarrhythmia or chest pain can signal excessive adrenergic effect.
priorities: Monitor ECG, BP, urine output, mental status, skin perfusion, and heart-failure signs.
Assess whether perfusion is improving without unacceptable tachycardia or ischemia.
Escalate ventricular ectopy, sustained tachyarrhythmia, chest pain, or worsening hypotension.
assessMonitor: Continuous ECG/BP; trend urine output, oxygenation, congestion, electrolytes, and invasive hemodynamics when available.
interventions: Use pump-controlled infusion and secure vascular access.
Correct severe hypovolemia before expecting an inotrope to solve low preload.
medicationSafety: Dobutamine can increase ectopic activity and heart rate.
Infusion titration should follow a critical-care order/protocol.
teaching: Explain that the drug supports heart pumping temporarily while the underlying cause is treated.
delegationScope: Inotrope titration requires defined critical-care competency; LPN/LVN authority varies by state/facility.
examTrap: Increasing dobutamine just because urine output is low without reassessing preload, rhythm, pressure, and overall perfusion.
oneLinePearl: Dobutamine should improve flow, not just make the heart beat faster.

title: Mannitol: Osmotic Diuresis and Volume Shifts
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV mannitol creates an osmotic shift that can reduce intracranial pressure but can also cause major fluid/electrolyte shifts, kidney injury, and pulmonary edema. Response must be judged using neurologic status, urine output, hemodynamics, osmolality/electrolytes, and lung findings.
recognize: Initial intravascular expansion may worsen pulmonary congestion before diuresis occurs.
Crystals can form in concentrated mannitol solutions and require product-specific inspection/handling.
priorities: Assess lungs, volume status, neurologic status, renal function, and urine output before and during therapy.
Use the ordered filter/administration method when required by product instructions.
Escalate anuria, worsening pulmonary edema, or neurologic decline.
assessMonitor: Trend serum electrolytes, osmolality when ordered, creatinine, urine output, BP, lung sounds, and neurologic response.
interventions: Inspect solution for crystals and follow warming/filter instructions when applicable.
Maintain accurate intake/output and weight trends.
medicationSafety: Current labeling warns against simultaneous administration with blood products through the same set because of pseudoagglutination/hemolysis risk.
Do not continue repeated doses blindly in worsening renal failure or volume overload.
teaching: Explain that frequent labs, urine measurements, and neurologic checks are part of safe therapy.
delegationScope: High-osmolar IV therapy requires facility competency; assessment of neurologic and volume response remains licensed-nurse responsibility.
examTrap: Giving another mannitol dose for rising ICP while ignoring new pulmonary edema and anuria.
oneLinePearl: Mannitol pulls water—but the lungs and kidneys decide whether that helps or harms.

title: Phenylephrine: Pressure Up, Perfusion Still Matters
bottomLine: Phenylephrine is primarily an alpha-1 agonist vasopressor used for clinically important vasodilatory hypotension in selected settings. It can raise blood pressure while causing reflex bradycardia and excessive vasoconstriction, so perfusion must be assessed along with the number on the monitor.
recognize: A rising BP with slowing heart rate can reflect reflex bradycardia.
Excess vasoconstriction may reduce peripheral or organ perfusion.
priorities: Monitor BP, heart rate/rhythm, mental status, urine output, skin temperature/color, and chest symptoms.
Verify concentration and pump setup before infusion or bolus administration.
Escalate severe bradycardia, ischemic symptoms, or worsening perfusion.
assessMonitor: Trend hemodynamics, perfusion, IV site, and response to correction of the underlying vasodilatory cause.
interventions: Use controlled administration according to setting-specific protocol.
Protect vascular access and assess extravasation risk.
medicationSafety: Concentrated products can require dilution; formulation matters.
Current 2026 labels include warnings for excessive vasoconstriction and product-specific sulfite reactions.
teaching: Explain that the medication temporarily supports blood pressure while the underlying cause is corrected.
delegationScope: Vasopressor administration/titration authority varies by state/facility and requires high-alert competency.
examTrap: Assuming improved blood pressure means improved perfusion when the patient becomes bradycardic and cool.
oneLinePearl: Phenylephrine raises pressure by squeezing vessels—always recheck perfusion.
